summaries.example: Imagine watching a balloon with dots drawn on it get bigger. The dots move farther apart as the balloon expands. Cosmologists use models like this to think about how space itself can expand. But the universe is not just one balloon among many that we can compare in a laboratory, so scientists must be careful when deciding what the evidence shows.
summaries.summary: Cosmology studies the physical universe as a whole. Its standard model says that the universe has expanded and cooled from an extremely hot early state, allowing structures such as galaxies and stars to develop. The model uses general relativity and adds ideas about dark matter, dark energy, and early-universe processes. It is supported by many different observations, including background radiation, light-element amounts, galaxy patterns, and measurements of expansion. Still, cosmology has special philosophical problems. We have only one universe, and light lets us observe only a limited part of it. Therefore, different models may agree about what we can see while disagreeing about distant regions or earlier times. The entry also discusses questions about the universe's beginning, the possible role of conditions that allow life, and how scientists should test theories when direct experiments may be impossible.
key_ideas: The standard cosmological model describes a universe that began very hot and dense, then expanded and cooled while stars and galaxies formed.
Cosmologists use general relativity, observations, and ideas about matter and energy to build this model.
The universe is unique, and we can observe only a limited region, so some large questions may have more than one reasonable answer.
The model fits many observations, but dark matter, dark energy, the earliest state, and some disagreements about measurements remain open questions.
Philosophers ask what counts as a good explanation when there is only one universe to study.
summaries.why_it_matters: Cosmology helps us understand the setting in which stars, planets, and life exist. It also teaches an important lesson about science: strong evidence can support a model without answering every question. Studying cosmology encourages us to separate what observations show from what a theory adds when it reaches beyond those observations.

important_terms.definition: The study of the physical universe, including its space, matter, history, and possible beginnings.
A carefully organized description used to explain observations and make predictions.
The idea that a scientific conclusion may not be forced by the evidence because different explanations can fit the same observations.
The idea that the universe has only one physical example, so we cannot compare it with other universes.
A proposed kind of matter that does not give off light but may help galaxies and other structures form.
A name for whatever may be causing the universe's expansion to speed up in the standard model.

questions_to_think_about: Why is studying one universe different from studying many examples of the same kind of object?
If two models fit the observations we have, what other reasons might help us choose between them?
What could a new observation show about the standard model?
Can a model be useful even if it does not answer every question?

summaries.example: Suppose two maps both reproduce every road visible from one town, but one map says the whole country is flat while the other says it curves dramatically beyond the horizon. The local evidence alone may not decide between them. Cosmology faces a related problem: observations along our past light cone can strongly constrain the universe we can see, yet may not determine its global structure. The standard FLRW models provide a highly symmetric description, but other models can imitate their observations over a limited region or period.
summaries.summary: The philosophy of cosmology examines what cosmological theories claim, how their evidence supports them, and where their limits lie. The contemporary standard model extends general relativity and other local physics to the universe as a whole. In its FLRW approximation, the universe expands through successive eras in which radiation, matter, and dark energy affect its dynamics differently. Small early irregularities grow into larger structures. Observations of background radiation, galaxy distributions, standard candles, nucleosynthesis, and other phenomena provide mutually reinforcing tests, although tensions such as differing expansion-rate measurements remain. The philosophical difficulty is that the universe is a unique object and that observation is restricted by horizons. A model can therefore be successful within our accessible region while differing elsewhere. This raises questions about the cosmological principle, global spacetime structure, and extrapolation. Singularity theorems indicate that many relativistic models are past-incomplete, but they do not settle the nature of the earliest state; quantum gravity may alter the conclusion. The entry also analyzes fine-tuning, observer-selection effects, multiverse proposals, and competing ideas about what counts as explanation in a one-universe science.
key_ideas: The standard model extends local physical theories to cosmic scales and is supported by several independent kinds of evidence, but it includes poorly understood ingredients such as dark matter, dark energy, and inflation.
FLRW geometry is powerful because of its symmetry, yet observations that look isotropic from our location do not automatically establish that the entire universe has that geometry.
Cosmology's unique subject and limited observational access create distinctive forms of underdetermination, including uncertainty about global structure and statistical anomalies.

Singularity theorems support a finite past for broad classes of relativistic models, but they do not describe the singularity's detailed structure or show that classical general relativity remains valid there.
Debates about initial conditions, fine-tuning, anthropic reasoning, and multiverse proposals concern both physical evidence and philosophical standards for explanation.
A good cosmological theory should do more than fit selected data; scientists also consider explanatory power, consistency with other theories, and the range of phenomena explained.
summaries.why_it_matters: Cosmology connects detailed physical theories with questions about the whole natural world. Its case studies show why evidence, assumptions, mathematical idealization, and explanatory standards must be examined together. They also caution against presenting speculative claims about origins, purpose, or other universes as if they had the same status as well-tested parts of the standard model.

important_terms.definition: A framework using general relativity and observations to describe cosmic expansion, cooling, structure formation, and the history of matter and radiation.
A curve in curved spacetime that plays the role of a straight path; freely falling bodies follow geodesics when no non-gravitational force acts.
The family of highly symmetric cosmological solutions in which space is homogeneous and isotropic, with expansion described by a scale factor.
The claim that available evidence may fit multiple theories or models, especially when those models differ outside the observed domain.
A limit on what can be observed or causally influenced because signals travel at a finite speed.
The fact that statistical predictions concern an ensemble of possible universes, while observations provide only one actual universe.
A breakdown or edge in the spacetime description where relevant curves cannot be extended and classical general relativity may cease to give a complete account.
Reasoning that accounts for the fact that observers can exist only under certain physical conditions; its rules and applications remain disputed.

questions_to_think_about: What additional evidence could distinguish a model that matches observations locally from one that also gives the correct global structure?
Why might agreement among different measurements provide stronger support than one successful prediction?
Does a singularity show that the universe began at a first moment, or only that a theory reaches a boundary of applicability?
When does anthropic reasoning explain an observation, and when might it merely describe a selection effect?
Should a theory that fits data but has little independent support be treated differently from one that unifies several phenomena?

summaries.example: Think of trying to understand a huge amusement park when you can stand in only one corner and see only as far as the park's walls allow. You might make an excellent map of your view, but you could still be unsure what lies beyond it. Cosmologists face something like this: observations support a universe that looks nearly smooth and expanding on very large scales, yet other models might copy those observations in the part we can see while differing elsewhere.
summaries.summary: Cosmology studies the universe's physical structure and history, while philosophy of cosmology asks how far our evidence and explanations can reach. The standard model describes a universe that expanded from a very hot early condition, cooled through different historical eras, and developed galaxies and other structures. It combines general relativity with observations and additional components such as dark matter, dark energy, and inflation. The model is supported because different methods—such as studying background radiation, light elements, galaxy patterns, and cosmic expansion—give broadly compatible results. However, the evidence does not automatically settle every question. We see only within horizons, and the universe is the only universe available for study. Thus, models can agree in our observable region while differing about distant or earlier parts. The entry examines this underdetermination, the status of highly symmetric FLRW models, the significance of past singularities, and the difficulty of explaining initial conditions. It also discusses anthropic reasoning and multiverse proposals as contested attempts to understand apparent fine-tuning. Finally, it asks what standards beyond simple data-fitting should guide theory choice.
key_ideas: The standard model describes an expanding, cooling universe in which matter and radiation pass through different stages and structures grow over time.
Its success comes from several kinds of observations that agree with one another, not from a single measurement.
The universe is unique, so cosmologists cannot compare it with other real universes in the ordinary way.
Our observations cover only a limited region and past history; models that agree there may disagree about the universe as a whole.
Philosophers debate whether unusual features need new physics, special initial conditions, observer-selection reasoning, or another explanation.
Cosmology must balance evidence with theory, because some ideas about the early universe cannot be tested directly in Earth-based experiments.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic matters because it shows how science works at the edge of observation. Cosmology gives us powerful knowledge about expansion and structure, but it also makes clear which conclusions depend on assumptions. Learning to identify evidence, extrapolation, and unresolved disagreement is useful in cosmology and in science more generally.

important_terms.definition: A scientific picture of the universe's large-scale history, including expansion, cooling, and the growth of galaxies and other structures.
The shape and structure of space and time, which general relativity treats as able to curve in response to matter and energy.
A very symmetrical model in which the universe has no special large-scale place or direction and is described by an expanding scale factor.
A problem that occurs when the evidence does not select just one theory because more than one explanation fits it.
A limit on what we can observe or affect because information cannot travel faster than light.
A possible kind of unseen matter that helps explain how galaxies and larger structures gather together.
An unknown component or effect used in the standard model to account for the universe's accelerated expansion.
A proposed set of many universes, often discussed as a possible way to address fine-tuning.

questions_to_think_about: Why does having only one universe make statistical reasoning difficult?
What is the difference between a model fitting observations and a model explaining them?
Why might a symmetrical model be useful even if the real universe has small irregularities?
What would count as independent evidence for dark matter?
How should scientists handle a theory that makes predictions only through uncertain assumptions about observers?
